title: Service of the heart (Taanit 2a)
hook: the Talmud calls prayer the service of the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayifga, and three times a day: morning, afternoon and evening, the hinges of the day. Did you find your three pauses? Today, what prayer is, in two Hebrew words. Day five hundred forty.

The Shema, said morning and evening, includes a paragraph from Deuteronomy that asks people to serve God with all their heart. Serve how, exactly? You can serve with your hands. You can build, carry, cook, bring an offering to an altar. That's what service meant in the Temple: real, physical work. But serve with your heart? You can't hand someone your heart on a plate. The Talmud stops at that phrase and asks exactly that question.
screen: `SERVE WITH YOUR HANDS.` → `BUILD, CARRY, COOK, OFFER.` → `BUT WITH YOUR HEART?`

segments.voice: The verse is Deuteronomy eleven: "to love the LORD your God, and to serve Him with all your heart and with all your soul." At the opening of tractate Taanit, the Talmud asks: what is service that is in the heart? And it answers: this is prayer. Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart. Avodah is the same word used for the priests' work in the Temple: the offerings, the incense, the daily routine. So the phrase makes a bold claim. Prayer is real service, standing alongside the Temple's. After the Temple was destroyed, that idea carried enormous weight: there was still a service anyone could bring, every day, with no altar at all. Where does the heart come in? The rabbis learned much about how to pray from Hannah, at the start of the book of Samuel, praying for a child. "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." The Talmud learns from her that prayer needs the heart directed, the lips moving, and the voice kept low. Jewish tradition has a word for that directing of the heart: kavanah, intention. The siddur supplies the words. The heart has to do the work of meaning them. That's why it's called service. It isn't only a feeling. It's effort, like any other work.
screen: `SERVE WITH ALL YOUR HEART.` · `AVODAH: THE TEMPLE'S WORK.` · `SERVICE WITHOUT AN ALTAR.` · `HANNAH: LIPS MOVING, VOICE UNHEARD.` · then, large: `PRAYER IS THE HEART'S WORK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one heartfelt sentence. Settle, and breathe. Let one sentence rise from somewhere honest in you. It could be thanks, a worry, a hope, a name. If you pray, it can be to God, in your own words. If you don't, it can be said to no one, or to the quiet. Say it the way Hannah did: lips moving, voice barely there. Then say it once more, slower, and mean every word. The bell holds the time.
Avodah shebalev. Service of the heart. The Talmud's name for prayer.
Your line: prayer is the heart's work. Today, out of the words you say on autopilot, mean one sentence completely. Day five hundred forty.

howItsDone: Jewish law asks for kavanah, focused intention, especially in the first line of the Shema and the first blessing of the Amidah, which is said quietly, lips moving, in the manner learned from Hannah.

original.note: Hebrew: service that is in the heart. the Talmud's name for prayer, Taanit 2a.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer is just a feeling.
what it means: prayer is service, real work, done with the heart.
what a scholar hears: Taanit 2a reads Deuteronomy 11:13 this way; avodah is the word for the Temple service, and Berakhot 31a learns prayer's manner from Hannah.
